summary: RW Aurigae is a known young star, about 509 light-years away, that sometimes dims when dust clouds pass in front of it. WANDERERS compared images from 2010 and 2026 and found a shift of about 0.6 arcseconds. That is under a tenth of a SPHEREx pixel, so the motion is too small to measure. From September 2025 to March 2026 its brightness changed by +0.03 ± 0.06 magnitudes, so it looked steady in these snapshots. Confidence is medium because the star is too bright for SPHEREx, which flagged 140 of 150 measurements.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: The card calls it steady because nothing changed beyond the noise in these snapshots. Its brightness rose only 0.03 magnitudes between Sep 2025 and Mar 2026, which is smaller than the ±0.06 uncertainty. Its position moved 0.57 arcseconds since 2010, less than a tenth of a SPHEREx pixel. Confidence is medium because 140 of 150 measurements are saturated, so brightness came from the star's faint outer glow. It can still dim at other times.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Most of this star's light overflows SPHEREx: 140 of 150 measurements are saturated, so brightness comes from the star's faint outer glow. The 0.06 mag uncertainty is bigger than the 0.03 mag change. There are only two snapshots, and RW Aurigae is known to dim unpredictably. The shift is under a tenth of a pixel. A third visit catching a dip would overturn "steady."

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this sky around 2010, and SPHEREx photographed it in 2025 and 2026. Together they give a 16-year gap for spotting motion. Here the shift was only 0.57 arcseconds, about a tenth of a SPHEREx pixel, which is too small to count as measured motion. SPHEREx also records many infrared colors. But RW Aurigae is too bright for it: 140 of 150 measurements are flagged, leaving 10 clean ones.
